name: Jamal Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior designer at Brennan Signs & Graphics, a small outfit of seven on the trading estate. We do logos, signs and van wraps for tradespeople: plumbers, roofers, builders. Most of my day is on the computer, drawing up a logo or laying a design over a van template. A couple of afternoons a week I help Gary, the owner, fit wraps in the unit, which means a heat gun, a squeegee and a lot of patience.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like seeing a van I wrapped go past on the main road, with a phone number I set in big letters. What wears me out is clients who want their logo bigger, then bigger again, until it's ugly. I use an AI tool now and then to show customers a mock-up of their van, but Gary still does the real designs better than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, honest work wins out in the end. At the trade counter I'd say the tradesmen were right not to worry. I don't post much online, just the odd van photo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. I'm still learning and Gary's patient with me. If nothing big changes, I can learn the trade properly from him, design and fitting both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Brennan's and ask Gary for more fitting days. I'd keep putting money aside, about three hundred a month, for a deposit with Lucia. I'd carry on using the mock-up tool, since customers like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled. Work's busy and money's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything weighing on you outside work in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Lucia works at her dad's bakery, which is steady, and my van's paid off. I've got about seven months of money put by. We're doing all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Gary think about AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary thinks it's a gimmick, mostly, though he likes the mock-ups. I half agree with him. No computer can fit a vinyl wrap round a wing mirror.

At the **trade counter** I'd say tradesmen were right not to worry.
think: I'm **relieved**, since I'm still learning from my boss.
I could learn **design and fitting** properly if nothing big changes.
do: Ask my boss for **more fitting days**.
Save about **three hundred** a month for a deposit with my girlfriend.
Keep using the **mock-up tool** for customers.

fieldNote: He splits his week between **screen design** and hands-on **fitting**.

steps.text: Ask Gary for more wrap fitting days each week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses have to keep up, that's the market. At the trade counter I'd say get your logo done by a person who'll stand behind it. I'd tell young lads to learn a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the logo and design side of my job shrinks a lot. Tradesmen will make their own logos on their phones. But wraps still need fitting, and Gary already says good fitters are hard to find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Gary to move me towards fitting, maybe three days a week instead of two. Once I saw other sign shops using AI for the designs, I'd learn it properly too. And I'd keep saving, maybe a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My income looks safe if I shift to fitting, but the design side I trained for is going. That's on my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You trained in design. Does it bother you to become mainly a fitter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. My mum was proud of the diploma. But a trade's a trade, and fitting is skilled. I'd rather earn with my hands than wait for a design job that isn't there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if design jobs disappear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. That's the market. If the government tries to stop it, it'll just go somewhere else. What I'd want is more apprenticeships, so young lads can learn fitting and signwriting.

I'd tell young lads to **learn a trade** and tradesmen to use a real designer.

**Fitting** still needs people, and good fitters are scarce.
do: Ask my boss for **three fitting days** a week.

feel: **Uneasy**, with income safe in fitting but his **design training** fading.

fieldNote: He blames **the market**, not anyone, and opposes heavy government action.
He's **ready to switch** to fitting despite pride in his diploma.
He wants more **apprenticeships**, in line with his views.

steps.text: Ask Gary for three wrap fitting days a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, and people need to roll up their sleeves. I wouldn't say wait for the government. At the trade counter I'd say every tradesman should get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my design work is gone by 2028. Fitting lasts until the robots, around 2031. Three years of fitting vinyl wraps isn't a career, but it's three years of wages, and in three years I can build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full-time on fitting at Brennan's straight away. I'd use my van to start fitting wraps on my own at weekends, for builders who know me. I'd put a few thousand into a proper heat gun kit and a vinyl stock. And I'd talk to Lucia's dad about whether the bakery needs help, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My income could go in a few years, but I can see what to do. I'm not panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens after 2031, when the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't really know. Maybe the robots fit wraps on new vans in factories, but old vans in a yard need a person for a while longer. Or I end up at the bakery with Lucia.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nights out and the new phone. Not the van, the van's my livelihood. We'd hold off on the deposit too.

I'd say **don't wait** for government, and tradesmen should get ready.
think: My **design work** is gone by 2028, and fitting lasts until robots.
**Three years** of fitting wages lets me build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to get ready, so get ready. I'd tell tradesmen to do the same. I'd say apprenticeships for fitters and signwriters matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I can build a small fitting business by 2031. The design job goes, but I'd have three more years as a fitter. That's eight years of earning, and that's enough to set up something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start weekend fitting in my second year, and maybe leave Brennan's by 2029 to go on my own. I'd save for a small unit. Lucia and I would marry and put down a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less. It's a plan. I like having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Leaving Gary sounds like a big risk. Is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, a bit. But I'd ask Gary first if he wants to partner, since he's near retirement. I'd rather buy into my boss's sign firm than compete with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about after 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be 35, with a business that might shrink. I'd hope we had a house and some savings by then. I can't plan past that, honestly.

I'd say **apprenticeships** for fitters and signwriters matter, and tradesmen should prepare too.
think: I can build a **fitting business** by 2031.

do: Offer to **buy into** the business with my boss.

feel: **Anxious**, but **less**, because he has a plan.

fieldNote: He'd **partner with his boss** rather than compete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no excuses. Learn a trade, save your money, look after your family. I'd say that to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel all right. By 2036 I'd be 37, maybe running Brennan's. The design side goes, but fitting carries on until 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Brennan's, learning fitting and the business side from Gary. I'd use AI tools for mock-ups as they get better. I'd save and invest in a share of the business by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's in the back of my mind, but I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the bit that still nags at you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm not that good at design, and I'll never get the chance to be. That's a bit sad. But wraps pay the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell young lads who want to design?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn to fit as well. A design diploma's nice, but a heat gun pays.

fieldNote: A decade lets him plan to **own part** of the firm.
He feels **quiet sadness** that his design skill will never mature.
He treats AI as a **useful tool** for mock-ups, not a threat.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's fast, and I'd lose design straight away and fitting soon after. What would help is apprenticeships and cheap start-up loans, so lads like me can set up on our own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the tradesmen. The tradesmen are my customers, and if the tradesmen are all right, I'm all right.

headlineQuote: The tradesmen are my customers, and if the tradesmen are all right, I'm all right.
portrait: Jamal is a **junior designer** at a sign and van-wrap firm for tradespeople.
He splits his week between **screen design** and hands-on **wrap fitting**.
He believes in **markets, trades** and family, not government help.
He plans to shift into **fitting** and maybe buy into his boss's firm.
He's **calm** in a plateau and **anxious** at most in the fast scenarios.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing design at once and fitting soon after.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** and cheap **start-up loans** for young tradespeople.
